steps.title: Recycle logic
steps.body: Single-pass conversion = reacted/fed to reactor. Overall conversion = reacted/fresh feed. A separator returning unreacted A makes overall conversion approach 100% even when single-pass is low.

steps.body: Fresh feed F = 100 mol/h A; all unreacted A is recycled; single-pass X = 0.5. Reactor feed = F + R. A reacted must equal 100 (overall X = 1), so 0.5(F + R) = 100, giving F + R = 200 and R = 100 mol/h.

steps.body: Put the balance boundary around the whole process for overall quantities and around the reactor or mixing point for internal ones; mixing the boundaries gives wrong equations.

lessons.title: Lab: Model a stirred tank from a mass balance

scenes.text: A dyeing unit in Surat switches the feed to a mixing tank from clear water to dye solution. The shift chemist must say how long until the outlet is nearly at feed colour.
She writes an unsteady component balance instead of guessing.

steps.title: Why dynamic models
steps.body: Steady-state balances say where a process ends up; **dynamic models** say how fast it gets there. The general balance is **accumulation = in − out + generation**. For a constant-volume, perfectly mixed tank (CSTR without reaction): V dC/dt = F(Cin − C). Define **time constant τ = V/F** (units: time). Then τ dC/dt + C = Cin.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
V = 2 m³, F = 0.1 m³/min, so τ = 20 min. Feed concentration steps from 0 to 1 kmol/m³ at t = 0 with C(0)=0.

Solution: C(t) = 1 − e^(−t/20). At t = 40 min: C = 1 − e^(−2) = 0.8647 kmol/m³, i.e. 86.5% of the way.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: How long to reach 95% of the change? 1 − e^(−t/τ) = 0.95 gives t = −τ ln(0.05) = 3τ ≈ 60 min. Rule of thumb: 63.2% at τ, 95% at 3τ, 99.3% at 5τ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using V/F with mismatched units (m³ vs L, min vs s).
- Forgetting to state the assumptions: perfect mixing, constant volume, constant density.
- Treating τ as the time to *finish*; it is the time to complete only 63.2%.

steps.body: L{f(t)} = ∫₀^∞ f(t)e^(−st)dt. Key pairs: **1 → 1/s**, **e^(−at) → 1/(s+a)**, **t → 1/s²**, **sin ωt → ω/(s²+ω²)**, δ(t) → 1. Derivative: L{dy/dt} = sY(s) − y(0); with deviation variables y(0)=0 so d/dt → s.

steps.title: Transfer function
steps.body: G(s) = Y(s)/X(s) for deviation variables with zero initial conditions. Linear process: Y = G·X. A first-order process τ dy/dt + y = Kx gives **G(s) = K/(τs + 1)**; K is the steady-state gain (output units per input units).

steps.title: Initial and final value theorems
steps.body: **Final value:** lim y(t) as t→∞ = lim s→0 of sY(s) (valid only if all poles of sY(s) lie in the left half-plane). **Initial value:** y(0⁺) = lim s→∞ of sY(s).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: 2 dy/dt + y = 3x. Transform: (2s+1)Y = 3X so G(s) = 3/(2s+1): K = 3, τ = 2.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Y(s) = 5/[s(3s+1)] for a unit-step-like input. Final value = lim s→0 of s·5/[s(3s+1)] = 5/1 = 5. Partial fractions: 5/s − 15/(3s+1) = 5/s − 5/(s+1/3), so y = 5(1 − e^(−t/3)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying the final value theorem to an unstable or oscillating Y(s) (e.g. poles on the imaginary axis) gives a meaningless number. Also, never carry initial conditions into a transfer function: use deviation variables.

lessons.title: Underdamped second-order response

steps.title: Standard form
steps.body: G(s) = K/(τ²s² + 2ζτs + 1) with natural frequency **ωn = 1/τ** and damping ratio **ζ**. Poles: s = −ζωn ± jωn√(1−ζ²). For 0<ζ<1 the step response oscillates; ζ = 1 critically damped; ζ > 1 overdamped (two real poles).

steps.title: Performance formulas (underdamped, unit step, K=1)
steps.body:
- Overshoot = exp(−πζ/√(1−ζ²))
- Decay ratio = (overshoot)²
- Peak time tp = π/(ωn√(1−ζ²))
- Rise time (first crossing of final value) = (π − φ)/(ωd), φ = cos⁻¹ζ
- Period of oscillation T = 2π/(ωn√(1−ζ²))
- Settling time (±2%) ≈ 4/(ζωn)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing ωn with the damped frequency ωd = ωn√(1−ζ²), and applying the overshoot formula when ζ ≥ 1 (no overshoot exists).

steps.title: Transfer function
steps.body: Non-interacting: the second tank does not affect the first. **G(s) = 1/[(τ1s+1)(τ2s+1)]** = 1/[τ1τ2 s² + (τ1+τ2)s + 1]. Compare with standard form: τ = √(τ1τ2), ζ = (τ1+τ2)/(2√(τ1τ2)) ≥ 1 (equality only if τ1 = τ2). Hence it is **always overdamped or critically damped**.

steps.title: Step response (τ1 ≠ τ2)
steps.body: y(t) = 1 − [τ1e^(−t/τ1) − τ2e^(−t/τ2)]/(τ1 − τ2). The response has an S-shape: zero initial slope, one inflection point, and is slower than a single tank.

steps.title: Interacting model
steps.body: With flow q1 = (h1 − h2)/R1 and q2 = h2/R2, A1 dh1/dt = q − q1 and A2 dh2/dt = q1 − q2. Eliminating gives **H2/Q = R2/[τ1τ2 s² + (τ1 + τ2 + A1R2)s + 1]**, τi = AiRi. The extra term **A1R2** is the interaction.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A1 = A2 = 1 m², R1 = R2 = 1 min/m². Non-interacting: s² + 2s + 1 → ζ = 1. Interacting: s² + (1+1+1)s + 1 = s² + 3s + 1, so 2ζτ = 3 with τ = 1 → **ζ = 1.5**: more sluggish.

steps.title: Key result
steps.body: For an interacting pair, the effective ζ is always > 1 and the response is slower than the non-interacting pair. The interacting model's two real roots are more widely separated than τ1 and τ2.

steps.title: Dead time
steps.body: Pure delay: y(t) = x(t − θ), transfer function **e^(−θs)**. For plug flow θ = L/v. A common process model is FOPDT: **G(s) = K e^(−θs)/(τs + 1)**. Dead time adds phase lag −ωθ without changing gain, and limits achievable control performance (θ/τ is a difficulty measure).

steps.title: Padé approximations
steps.body: 1st order: e^(−θs) ≈ (1 − θs/2)/(1 + θs/2). 2nd order: (1 − θs/2 + θ²s²/12)/(1 + θs/2 + θ²s²/12). The Padé numerator creates a **right-half-plane zero at s = 2/θ**, mimicking the delay for analysis but giving initial inverse response.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: L = 50 m, v = 2 m/s gives θ = 25 s. First-order Padé zero at 2/25 = 0.08 s⁻¹.

steps.title: Worked example 2

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Believing a Padé approximation is exact; it is accurate only at low frequencies (ωθ < ~1 for 1st order).

steps.title: Method (Smith's two-point)

steps.title: The three modes
steps.body: **PID (ideal):** Gc = Kc[1 + 1/(τI s) + τD s]. Integral (reset) removes offset; τI in min/repeat, reset rate = 1/τI. Derivative anticipates, adds phase lead, amplifies noise; usually filtered: τD s/(ατD s + 1) with α ≈ 0.1.

steps.title: PI on a first-order process
steps.body: With Gp = K/(τs+1): characteristic equation ττI s² + τI(1+KKc)s + KKc = 0, so **ωn² = KKc/(ττI)** and **2ζωn = (1+KKc)/τ**. The closed loop is second order, so it can oscillate even though the plant cannot.

steps.title: Practical rules
steps.body: Flow and pressure loops: PI, fast. Level (averaging): P or loose PI. Temperature: PI or PID. Composition with long dead time: PI, small Kc, careful with D.

steps.body: Reducing τI to make the loop 'faster': a small τI means strong integral action and more oscillation. Another is setting derivative on noisy flow signals.

story.title: How the poles move as gain grows

steps.title: Root locus idea
steps.body: Plot the roots of 1 + K·G(s)H(s) = 0 as K goes from 0 to ∞. Rules: (1) branches start at open-loop poles, end at zeros (or ∞); (2) number of branches = number of poles; (3) on the real axis, the locus lies to the left of an odd number of poles+zeros; (4) **asymptote angles** (2k+1)180°/(n−m); (5) **centroid** = (Σpoles − Σzeros)/(n−m); (6) breakaway points from dK/ds = 0; (7) imaginary-axis crossing by Routh.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: GH = K/[s(s+1)(s+2)]: poles 0, −1, −2; n−m = 3 so asymptotes at ±60° and 180°; centroid = (0−1−2)/3 = **−1**. K = −s(s+1)(s+2) = −(s³+3s²+2s); dK/ds = −(3s²+6s+2) = 0 → s = −0.423 (on locus, between 0 and −1) and −1.577 (not on locus). Routh: s³ + 3s² + 2s + K: s¹ element (6 − K)/3 → **K = 6**, auxiliary 3s² + 6 = 0 → ω = √2 = 1.414.

steps.title: Reading the locus
steps.body: For K < 6 all poles are in the LHP: stable. For K > 6 two branches cross into the RHP. The locus also shows damping: a radial line from the origin at angle θ with cosθ = ζ marks constant damping.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using a breakaway root that is not on the locus (here −1.577 lies to the left of an even count) and mixing up asymptote number n−m.

lessons.title: Gain margin and phase margin

scenes.text: A new loop works but a colleague worries it is 'too close to oscillation'.
Margins quantify how much extra gain or lag it can tolerate.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **Phase crossover ωc180:** frequency where φOL = −180°. **Gain margin GM = 1/AR_OL(ωc180)** (and 20 log GM in dB); the loop gain may be multiplied by GM before instability. **Gain crossover ωgc:** where AR_OL = 1. **Phase margin PM = 180° + φOL(ωgc)**, the extra lag tolerated before instability.

steps.title: Design guidance
steps.body: Typical: **GM > 1.7 (≈ 4.6 dB)** and **PM = 30°–45°**. Large margins mean sluggish loops, small margins mean oscillation. Margins give robustness to model error and dead-time uncertainty: extra delay Δθ tolerated ≈ PM(rad)/ωgc.

lessons.title: Nyquist stability criterion

scenes.text: A research student plots G(jω) in the complex plane and watches how it passes the point −1.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body: Plot GOL(jω) for ω from −∞ to +∞ (a closed contour for the Nyquist path). **Z = N + P**: Z = closed-loop RHP poles, P = open-loop RHP poles, N = clockwise encirclements of **−1 + 0j**. For a stable open loop (P = 0) the closed loop is stable if the curve **does not encircle −1**.

steps.title: Relation to Bode
steps.body: Crossing the negative real axis at −1/GM gives the gain margin; the angle at |G| = 1 gives PM. The Bode form of the criterion: for stable open loop, AR < 1 at ωc180 ⇔ stable.

steps.title: Worked example 1

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: An open-loop unstable plant has P = 1; stable closed loop requires N = −1, i.e. one **counter-clockwise** encirclement.

steps.title: Common mistake

scenes.text: A furnace outlet temperature drifts every time fuel-gas pressure changes, and the feedback loop reacts only after the product is off-spec.
The engineer proposes a flow cascade and a feedforward correction.

steps.title: Strategies
steps.body:
- **Cascade:** the primary (master) controller sets the set-point of a faster secondary (slave) loop. The inner loop rejects disturbances before they reach the primary; the inner loop should be at least 3–5 times faster.
- **Feedforward:** measure the disturbance and act at once: **Gff = −Gd/Gp** (ideal). Realisable with lead–lag and dead-time compensation; typically combined with feedback trim.
- **Ratio control:** keep flow B = R × flow A (air/fuel). **Split-range**, **override/selector** controls, and **inferential** control complete the toolbox.

rounds.q: A temperature loop oscillates after a controller replacement. How do you investigate?
rounds.model: First confirm the loop is in the right action and mode. Look at the trend: constant-amplitude oscillation suggests gain too high or stiction. I would reduce Kc, check valve behaviour with a small manual step, check sensor response and, if needed, retune using a bump test. I would log the change and inform the operator.

rounds.q: Explain why proportional-only control gives offset.
rounds.model: At a new steady state the valve must be at a new position. With P-only, output = bias + Kc e, so a non-zero e is needed. Higher Kc reduces it but cannot eliminate it. Integral action keeps changing the output until e = 0.

rounds.q: What is a Bode plot's use in control?
rounds.model: A Bode plot shows amplitude ratio and phase of the open loop against frequency. From it I read gain and phase margins to judge stability and robustness and choose a controller gain.

rounds.q: Describe a time you handled a mistake at work or in a lab.
rounds.model: In a lab I misread a rotameter scale and my data were off. I told my partner, repeated the measurement with a calibration check and added a double-check step to our procedure. We finished on time and the report was accurate.

rounds.q: Why choose a feedforward in addition to feedback?
rounds.model: Feedforward acts when the disturbance is measured, before the output moves, so it reduces the peak error. Because models are imperfect it is combined with feedback trim that removes the remaining offset.

lessons.title: Modes of heat transfer and Fourier's law

scenes.text: A steel kettle boils on a stove. The handle slowly gets warm although it never touches the flame.
Across the room, sunlight warms your face through the window without heating the air in between.
A process engineer must name each mechanism before she can size an exchanger: conduction, convection or radiation.

steps.title: Three modes and Fourier's law
steps.body:
**Conduction:** energy moves through a stationary medium by molecular/electron interaction. **Convection:** energy carried by bulk fluid motion plus conduction (Newton's law: q = h A (Ts − T∞)). **Radiation:** electromagnetic emission, needs no medium (Stefan–Boltzmann: q = ε σ A T⁴, σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴).

**Fourier's law (1-D):** q_x = −k A dT/dx. The heat flux q″ = q/A (W/m²) flows from high to low temperature; k is thermal conductivity (W/m·K). Typical k: copper ≈ 385, mild steel ≈ 45, brick ≈ 0.7, water ≈ 0.6, air ≈ 0.026.

For a plane wall of thickness L with faces at T1 and T2 (steady, constant k): **q = k A (T1 − T2)/L**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · brick wall
steps.body:
A brick wall (k = 0.72 W/m·K) is 0.2 m thick with faces at 130 °C and 30 °C. Find flux and the rate through 10 m².
- Step 1: ΔT = 100 K
- Step 2: q″ = kΔT/L = 0.72 × 100 / 0.2 = **360 W/m²**
- Step 3: q = 360 × 10 = **3600 W**

steps.title: Solved example 2 · copper plate
steps.body:
Copper (k = 385 W/m·K), L = 0.05 m, ΔT = 20 K.
- q″ = 385 × 20 / 0.05 = 154 000 W/m² = **154 kW/m²**
The same plate in firebrick (k = 1) would pass only 400 W/m² — conductivity differences of 2–3 orders of magnitude are why metals are used for exchangers and bricks for furnaces.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the minus sign's meaning: heat flows DOWN the gradient; use |ΔT| for magnitude.
- Using temperatures in °C inside T⁴ radiation formulas — use kelvin.
- Mixing k (W/m·K) with h (W/m²·K).
- Treating thickness in cm or mm without converting to metres.

steps.title: Electrical analogy
steps.body:
Heat rate q = ΔT / R_total. Resistances: conduction slab **R = L/(kA)**; convection **R = 1/(hA)**. Layers in series add: R_tot = ΣR. Flux through all series layers is the same, so each layer's ΔT = q·R_layer.

Parallel paths: 1/R = Σ 1/R_i. Overall coefficient: **U = 1/(1/h_i + ΣL/k + 1/h_o)** with q = U A ΔT_overall.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding conductivities instead of resistances.
- Forgetting the convective film resistances at the surfaces.
- Using ΔT across one layer with the total R.
- Ignoring contact resistance between rough surfaces when the problem gives it.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
For a long cylinder, steady, no generation, heat rate Q is constant but area A = 2πrL varies: Q = −k(2πrL)dT/dr. Separate and integrate from r_i to r_o:

**Q = 2πkL (T_i − T_o) / ln(r_o/r_i)**, so R_cyl = ln(r_o/r_i)/(2πkL).

For multiple layers add ln(r_{j+1}/r_j)/(2πk_jL). Temperature profile is logarithmic. Overall coefficient is referred to an area: U_o A_o = 1/ΣR.

steps.body:

- ln(0.08/0.03) = 0.9808
- Q = 2π×0.06×1×160 / 0.9808 = 60.32/0.9808 ≈ **61.5 W**

steps.body:

- Forgetting that flux q″ differs at each radius though Q is constant.

steps.title: Sphere and critical radius
steps.body:
Sphere: **Q = 4πk (T_i − T_o)/(1/r_i − 1/r_o)**.

Adding insulation to a small cylinder raises conduction resistance (ln r) but lowers outside convective resistance (area grows). Total R = ln(r/r_i)/(2πkL) + 1/(2πrLh). Setting dR/dr = 0 gives the **critical radius**:
- Cylinder: **r_c = k/h**
- Sphere: **r_c = 2k/h**
If r_o < r_c, insulation increases loss until r = r_c; if r_o ≥ r_c, any insulation reduces loss.

steps.body: Insulation k = 0.17 W/m·K, h = 8 W/m²K, cylinder: r_c = 0.17/8 = 0.02125 m = **21.25 mm**. A 10 mm radius electric wire should be insulated beyond 21.25 mm to be useful as a heat-loss barrier; below that, insulation works as a cooling aid — which is desirable for wires.

steps.body:

- Applying critical radius to large steam pipes, where r_o ≫ r_c and insulation always helps.

steps.title: Governing equation and results
steps.body:
Heat generation q‴ (W/m³) from electric current, nuclear fission or exothermic reaction. 1-D steady equation: d²T/dx² + q‴/k = 0 (slab); (1/r)d/dr(r dT/dr) + q‴/k = 0 (cylinder).

With surface at T_s: slab half-thickness L: **T_max − T_s = q‴L²/(2k)**; solid cylinder radius R: **T_max − T_s = q‴R²/(4k)**; solid sphere: **q‴R²/(6k)**. Surface temperature from energy balance: T_s = T_∞ + q‴V/(hA).

steps.body: Plate half-thickness 20 mm, q‴ = 10⁶, k = 10: ΔT = 10⁶×(0.02)²/(2×10) = 400/20 = **20 K**. If h = 500 W/m²K and fluid 80 °C: flux at face = q‴L = 20 000 W/m²; T_s = 80 + 20 000/500 = 120 °C; T_max = **140 °C**.

steps.body:

- Taking L as full thickness for the slab formula (it is half-thickness with both faces cooled).

steps.title: Fin equation
steps.body:
An energy balance on a thin fin element (cross-section A_c, perimeter P, conduction along the fin, convection from the surface) gives

**d²θ/dx² − m²θ = 0**, θ = T − T∞, **m = √(hP/kA_c)** (1/m).

Base θ_b. Solutions: infinitely long fin q = √(hPkA_c) θ_b. **Insulated tip:** q = √(hPkA_c) θ_b tanh(mL). Convective tip: use corrected length L_c = L + A_c/P (valid for small h).

steps.title: Dimensions, units and systems
steps.body:
A **dimension** is a physical nature (length L, mass M, time T, temperature Θ, amount N). A **unit** is a chosen scale of a dimension.

- **SI:** m, kg, s, K, mol. Derived: N = kg·m/s², Pa = N/m², J = N·m, W = J/s.
- **CGS:** cm, g, s. dyne = g·cm/s², erg = dyne·cm.
- **FPS (English engineering):** ft, lbm, s, °F/°R. 1 lbf is the force that gives 1 lbm an acceleration of 32.174 ft/s², so g_c = 32.174 lbm·ft/(lbf·s²).

**Dimensional homogeneity:** every term added or equated in an equation must have the same dimensions. Arguments of log, exp and trig functions must be dimensionless.

steps.title: Conversion factors worth memorising
steps.body:
- 1 atm = 101.325 kPa = 1.01325 bar = 760 mmHg = 14.696 psi
- 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa
- 1 cal = 4.184 J (thermochemical); 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ
- 1 hp = 745.7 W; 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ
- 1 lb = 0.4536 kg; 1 ft = 0.3048 m; 1 gal (US) = 3.785 L
- R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) = 8.314 kPa·m³/(kmol·K) = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K)

Technique: multiply by conversion factors written as fractions equal to 1, and cancel units like algebra.

steps.body:

Check: 1 kW ≈ 860 kcal/h, so 250 kcal/h ≈ 0.29 kW ✓.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Mole:** amount containing 6.022×10²³ entities. 1 mol = M grams; 1 kmol = M kg; 1 lbmol = M lb.
- Moles n = m / M.
- **Mass fraction** w_i = m_i / m_total; **mole fraction** x_i = n_i / n_total (y_i for gases).
- Σ w_i = 1 and Σ x_i = 1.
- **Average molecular weight:** M̄ = Σ x_i M_i (a mole-weighted average) and 1/M̄ = Σ (w_i / M_i).

For air, 0.79 N₂ + 0.21 O₂ gives M̄ ≈ 28.84 kg/kmol.

steps.title: Method for converting composition
steps.body: Take a basis of **100 kg** (to go mass → mole) or **100 kmol** (mole → mass). Tabulate component, mass, M, moles, then divide by totals. Never convert fractions directly; always go through absolute amounts.

- Forgetting that kmol and kg differ by M (not the same number).

steps.title: Ideal gas equation

steps.title: Pressure and temperature
steps.body:

- Manometer: ΔP = ρ g h. A 200 mm column of mercury (13 600 kg/m³) gives 13600×9.81×0.2 = 26.7 kPa.

**Flow rates:** mass ṁ (kg/h), molar ṅ (kmol/h), volumetric V̇ (m³/h): ṁ = ρ V̇; ṅ = ṁ/M.

steps.title: Choosing a basis
steps.body:
The **basis** is the reference quantity for the calculation (e.g. 100 kg feed, 1 h of operation, 100 kmol gas). Choose:
- the given stream flow rate if one exists,
- 100 (kg/kmol) if composition fractions are given,
- 1 mol of a reactant for stoichiometry.
Results can be scaled afterwards. A flowsheet should label every stream with flow, composition, T, P and phase.

lessons.title: Lab: Stoichiometry, limiting and excess reactants

scenes.text: A burner is fed methane and oxygen, and the operator asks how much air is too much.
Pooja finds the limiting reactant before writing any balance.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
A balanced equation, e.g. **N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃**, gives stoichiometric coefficients ν.

- **Stoichiometric ratio:** mole ratio required by the equation (N₂:H₂ = 1:3).
- **Limiting reactant:** the one present in the smallest stoichiometric proportion; it determines the maximum extent of reaction.
- **Excess reactant:** present beyond the stoichiometric need.
- **% excess = (n_fed − n_stoich) / n_stoich × 100**, where n_stoich is the amount needed to react completely with the *limiting* reactant.

Compare feed ÷ coefficient for each reactant: the smallest ratio identifies the limiting reactant.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · N₂ + 3H₂
steps.body:
Feed 100 mol N₂ and 200 mol H₂.
- Ratios: N₂ 100/1 = 100; H₂ 200/3 = 66.7 → **H₂ is limiting**.
- N₂ needed for 200 mol H₂ = 66.67 mol; excess N₂ = 33.33 mol.
- % excess N₂ = 33.33/66.67 = **50 %**.
- Maximum NH₃ = 200 × 2/3 = 133.3 mol.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Methane burner
steps.body:
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Feed 5 mol CH₄ and 12 mol O₂.
- O₂ needed = 10 mol; supplied 12 → CH₄ is limiting.
- % excess O₂ = (12 − 10)/10 = **20 %**.
- Products at complete reaction: 5 CO₂, 10 H₂O, 2 O₂ unreacted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing % excess relative to the amount fed instead of the amount required.
- Choosing the limiting reactant by smaller moles instead of smaller moles ÷ coefficient.
- Using a mass ratio without converting through molecular weights.

steps.title: Performance measures
steps.body:
- **Fractional conversion X = (moles reacted)/(moles fed)** of a reactant.
- **Yield (basis feed):** moles of desired product formed / moles of limiting reactant fed (with stoichiometric correction ν_A/ν_P when needed).
- **Fractional yield (selectivity-based):** moles of desired product formed / moles of the limiting reactant reacted (adjusted for ν).
- **Selectivity S = moles of desired product / moles of undesired product.**
- **Single-pass conversion** (per pass through the reactor) vs **overall conversion** (whole process with recycle).

steps.body:

- Fractional yield (on reacted) = 60/80 = **0.75**
- Selectivity B/C = 60/20 = **3**.

steps.title: Three methods
steps.body:
1. **Molecular species balance:** include a generation/consumption term for each compound.
2. **Extent of reaction ξ (mol):** n_i = n_i0 + ν_i ξ, with ν negative for reactants, positive for products. For several reactions: **n_i = n_i0 + Σ_j ν_ij ξ_j**.
3. **Atomic balance:** atoms C, H, O, N… are conserved: Σ atoms in = Σ atoms out. No reaction rates or stoichiometry needed; good for combustion with many products.

DOF with reactions: unknowns − (independent species balances or atomic balances + extra relations).

steps.body:
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Feed 10 mol N₂, 30 mol H₂; N₂ conversion 40 %.
- ξ = 0.4 × 10 = 4 mol
- N₂ = 6, H₂ = 30 − 12 = 18, NH₃ = 8; total 32 mol
- y(NH₃) = 8/32 = **0.25**.

steps.title: Single-pass vs overall conversion
steps.body:
- **Single-pass conversion:** (reactant consumed in the reactor) / (reactant fed to the reactor).
- **Overall conversion:** (reactant consumed in the process) / (fresh reactant fed to the process).

With recycle, the overall conversion can be near 100 % even if single-pass conversion is low. A **separator** removes product; unreacted reactants return. If the fresh feed contains **inerts**, they accumulate, so a **purge** is taken from the recycle; at steady state the inerts in the purge equal those in the fresh feed (when none leave elsewhere).

- Reactor N₂ feed F: 0.25 F = 100 → **F = 400 mol/h**; recycle N₂ = 300.
- Reactor H₂ feed = 1200 mol/h; NH₃ made = 200 mol/h.

lessons.title: Lab: Real gases — compressibility and van der Waals

story.title: The cylinder that is not ideal

scenes.text: CO₂ at 5 MPa is stored in a cylinder; the ideal gas law over-predicts the volume.
Tara fixes the error with a compressibility factor.

steps.title: Departure from ideality
steps.body:
At high pressure or low temperature, molecular volume and attractions matter.

- **Compressibility factor Z = PV/(nRT)**. Z = 1 for an ideal gas; Z < 1 where attraction dominates; Z > 1 where repulsion dominates (very high P).
- **Real-gas form:** PV = ZnRT.
- **van der Waals:** (P + a n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, or per mole P = RT/(V − b) − a/V². b accounts for finite size, a for attraction.
- **Law of corresponding states:** Z is nearly the same function of reduced properties T_r = T/T_c and P_r = P/P_c for all gases. For mixtures use **Kay's rule** with pseudo-critical properties T_c′ = Σ y_i T_ci, P_c′ = Σ y_i P_ci.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Z-factor
steps.body:
2 kmol of gas at 300 K and 5000 kPa with Z = 0.90.
- Ideal V = nRT/P = 2×8.314×300/5000 = 0.998 m³.
- Real V = Z × ideal = **0.898 m³**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · van der Waals pressure
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using gauge pressure in Z.

steps.title: Vapour pressure
steps.body:
**Vapour pressure p\*** is the pressure at which vapour and liquid coexist at a given T; the **boiling point** is where p\* = external pressure.

- **Antoine:** log₁₀ p\* = A − B/(C + T). For water (p in mmHg, T in °C, 1–100 °C): A = 8.07131, B = 1730.63, C = 233.426.
- **Clausius–Clapeyron:** ln(p₂/p₁) = −(ΔH_v/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁), assuming constant ΔH_v.
- **Raoult's law (ideal liquid):** p_i = x_i p_i\*, and y_i P = x_i p_i\*.
- **Bubble point:** Σ x_i p_i\* = P. **Dew point:** Σ y_i P/p_i\* = 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C or inconsistent pressure units in Antoine constants.
- Applying Raoult's law to strongly non-ideal mixtures.
- Forgetting that vapour composition differs from liquid composition.

steps.title: Humidity terms (air–water vapour)

steps.title: Henry's law
steps.body:
For a sparingly soluble gas: **p_i = H x_i** (H in bar or kPa for mole-fraction basis; higher H = less soluble; H increases with T). Raoult's law applies to the solvent, Henry's law to the dilute solute.

A gas **saturated** with a vapour at T has partial pressure p\*(T) of that vapour: y = p\*/P; moles of vapour per mole dry gas = p\*/(P − p\*).

Dissolved gas per kg of water: n = x/(1 − x) × 55.51 mol.

steps.body:

- mol per kg water = 1.198×10⁻³/(1−0.0012) × 55.51 = 0.0666 mol → **2.9 g CO₂ per kg water**.

lessons.title: Lab: First law for closed and open systems

story.title: How much heat does the water heater need?

scenes.text: A heater raises 2 kg/s of water from 20 °C to 80 °C.

steps.title: Energy forms and the first law
steps.body:
Total energy = internal U + kinetic KE + potential PE. Heat Q and work W are energy in transit (not properties). Sign convention used here: **Q positive into the system, W positive done by the system**.

- **Closed system:** ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE = Q − W.
- **Open, steady-flow:** Q − W_s = ΔH + ΔKE + ΔPE (per unit time with flow rates), where **H = U + PV** is enthalpy; W_s is shaft work.
- Many process problems have negligible ΔKE and ΔPE: **Q = ΔH** if W_s = 0.
- Enthalpy is a state function; only differences matter: choose a **reference state** and compute ΔH along any convenient path.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Adiabatic turbine
steps.body:
Steam enters at h = 3200 kJ/kg and leaves at 2500 kJ/kg at 5 kg/s. Q = 0, ΔKE, ΔPE neglected.
- Ẇ_s = −ṁΔh = −5×(2500 − 3200) = **3500 kW** produced.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up the sign conventions of Q and W (check the textbook convention).
- Using Q = ΔU for an open system (it should be ΔH).
- Ignoring a shaft work that is not negligible (pump, compressor).

steps.title: Heat capacity and sensible heat
steps.body:
**Sensible heat** changes T without phase change: **Q = ∫ n C_p dT**. Heat capacity is often a polynomial: C_p = a + bT + cT² + dT³. For constant C_p: Q = n C_p ΔT. A **mean** C_p between T₁ and T₂ is the integral divided by ΔT.

For ideal gases C_p − C_v = R. For liquids and solids C_p ≈ C_v.

**Latent heat:** heat for a phase change at constant T and P: ΔH_fus (melting), ΔH_vap (boiling), ΔH_sub (sublimation). Water at 1 atm: ΔH_fus ≈ 334 kJ/kg; ΔH_vap(100 °C) ≈ 2257 kJ/kg (40.66 kJ/mol).

When a phase change occurs, break the path into: sensible heat to the transition T, latent heat, sensible heat after.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Draw the flowsheet and mark all inlet/outlet T, P, phase and flow.
2. Choose reference states (e.g. liquid water at 0 °C).
3. Compute specific enthalpy of each stream relative to the reference (tables or c_p).
4. Write Σ ṁ_out h_out − Σ ṁ_in h_in = Q̇ − Ẇ_s.

**Heat exchanger (no heat loss):** ṁ_h c_h (T_hi − T_ho) = ṁ_c c_c (T_co − T_ci).
**Mixing of liquids (ideal):** T_mix = Σ(ṁ_i c_i T_i)/Σ(ṁ_i c_i).
**Steam as a heating medium:** condensing steam releases its latent heat at nearly constant T — e.g. saturated steam at 1 atm gives ≈2257 kJ/kg.
**Mixing with heat of solution:** add Δ H_soln when relevant (strong acids/bases).

steps.title: Standard heats of reaction
steps.body:
**Standard heat of reaction ΔH°rxn** (at 25 °C, 1 bar) = Σ ν_i ΔH°f,i (products) − Σ ν_i ΔH°f,i (reactants). ΔH°f of elements in their standard state = 0.

- Exothermic: ΔH < 0; endothermic: ΔH > 0.
- **Heat of combustion:** ΔH°c; product water liquid gives **higher heating value (HHV)**, water vapour gives **lower heating value (LHV)**.
- **Hess's law:** ΔH of a net reaction = sum of ΔH of its steps.
- **Kirchhoff:** ΔH°(T) = ΔH°(298) + ∫₂₉₈^T ΔC_p dT, with ΔC_p = Σ ν C_p (products) − Σ ν C_p (reactants).

Data (kJ/mol): CH₄ −74.8; CO₂ −393.5; H₂O(l) −285.8; H₂O(g) −241.8.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Methane HHV and LHV
steps.body:
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
- HHV (liquid water): −393.5 + 2(−285.8) − (−74.8) = **−890.3 kJ/mol**
- LHV (steam): −393.5 + 2(−241.8) − (−74.8) = **−802.3 kJ/mol**
- Difference = 2 × 44 kJ/mol latent heat of water.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Hess's law
steps.body:
C + O₂ → CO₂: −393.5. CO + ½O₂ → CO₂: −283.0.
- C + ½O₂ → CO = −393.5 − (−283.0) = **−110.5 kJ/mol** (cannot be measured directly).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing the sign (products − reactants).
- Using H₂O(l) when the reaction gives water vapour.
- Forgetting stoichiometric coefficients.

lessons.title: Lab: Reactor energy balances and adiabatic temperature

scenes.text: An exothermic reaction releases 50 kJ per mole converted.
Without cooling the temperature climbs. Vikram computes the adiabatic temperature rise.

steps.title: Reactive energy balance (extent-of-reaction method)
steps.body:
Q̇ = ξ̇ ΔH°rxn + Σ ṅ_out Ĥ_out − Σ ṅ_in Ĥ_in

where Ĥ is the enthalpy of each species relative to the reference (25 °C, elements or reactants & products as chosen). With constant C_p:
- **Isothermal reactor at the reference T:** Q̇ = ξ̇ ΔH°rxn.
- **Adiabatic (Q = 0):** ξ̇ (−ΔH°rxn) = Σ ṅ_out C_p (T_ad − T_ref) (with inlet at T_ref). Hence **T_ad = T_ref + ξ̇(−ΔH)/(ΣṅC_p)**.

The adiabatic flame temperature is the T reached by combustion products without heat loss; it ignores dissociation, so measured temperatures are lower.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Isothermal cooled reactor
steps.body:
A → B at 298 K, ΔH = −50 kJ/mol, feed 10 mol/s, X = 0.8.
- ξ̇ = 8 mol/s → Q̇ = 8 × (−50) = **−400 kW** (400 kW of heat must be removed).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Adiabatic operation
steps.body:
Same reaction, adiabatic, feed at 298 K; mean total heat capacity 100 J/mol·K per mole of stream (10 mol/s).
- Heat released = 400 kW
- Σ ṅ C_p = 10 × 100 = 1000 W/K
- ΔT = 400 000/1000 = 400 K → **T_ad = 698 K**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Sizing cooling water
steps.body:
To remove the 400 kW with water that heats by 10 K (c_p 4.18):
- ṁ = 400/(4.18×10) = **9.57 kg/s**.

steps.body:
- Using ΔH_rxn at the wrong temperature without correcting.
- Forgetting that ΔH × ξ uses moles of reaction, not moles of feed.
- Ignoring heat capacity of inerts (N₂ in air).
